title: Audit new step arguments added since the last release for backwards compatibility
description:
A number of steps gained new arguments in the current development version (see the `NEWS.md` bullets for #58, #166, #171, #173, #174, #234, #253, #270, #325, and any others added before release). Before releasing, we should go through each of them and confirm they were added in a backwards-compatible way.

Things to check for each new argument:

* The new argument is added *after* the existing arguments in the step's formals, so positional calls written against the previous release still resolve to the same arguments.
* The default reproduces the previous behavior exactly, so existing recipes give identical results.
* `step_*_new()` and `prep()` carry the field through, and `bake()` tolerates its absence (e.g. via `isTRUE()`/`%||%`) so recipes prepped and saved with the previous release still bake.
* The corresponding direct-implementation function (where one exists) is consistent with the step.
* Tunable parameters and `tunable()` output are unchanged unless intentionally extended.

A short checklist run over the full list would be enough to catch any that slipped through.

title: Allow per-class targets in over_ratio/under_ratio (named vector) for multiclass control
description:
## Current behavior

The over-sampling steps take a single scalar `over_ratio` and the under-sampling steps take a single scalar `under_ratio`. The target count is derived from one reference class (the majority for `over_ratio`, the minority for `under_ratio`) and applied uniformly to every other class, as described in the ratio article. There is no way to give different classes different targets.

## Limitation

In multiclass problems with heterogeneous imbalance this is restrictive. A user may want to bring one class up substantially while nudging another only slightly, or keep different numbers of rows per majority class. Today that is not expressible.

For reference, imbalanced-learn's `sampling_strategy` accepts, in addition to a float and string modes, a per-class dict of explicit target counts and a callable returning such a dict, which is what enables "bring class A to 500, B to 300".

## Proposal

Allow `over_ratio`/`under_ratio` to accept a named numeric vector in addition to the current scalar. Names are class levels; the scalar path stays exactly as-is for backward compatibility.

## Design questions (worth a design pass before implementing)

- Counts vs ratios: should vector values be explicit per-class target counts, or per-class ratios relative to the reference class? The current scalar is a ratio; imbalanced-learn's dict is explicit counts. Pick one and document it clearly.
- Over vs under semantics: for over-sampling a target cannot be below the current count (you cannot delete rows); for under-sampling it cannot exceed the current count. Validation should mirror the existing scalar behavior per direction.
- Unspecified classes: what happens to a class not named in the vector? Left untouched, or fall back to the scalar/default target.
- Interaction with `tunable()`/dials: a scalar `over_ratio()`/`under_ratio()` is a tunable parameter, but a per-class vector is not naturally a single tunable value. Decide how tuning and per-class targets coexist (for example, supplying a vector opts out of tuning for that step).
- Edge cases: names that do not match any level, missing names, and unused (zero-count) factor levels.

This is the biggest expressiveness gap relative to per-class targeting, but the `tunable()` interaction is the tricky part, so it deserves a design pass first.

title: Add NearMiss-2 and NearMiss-3 variants to step_nearmiss()
description:
The current `step_nearmiss()` / `nearmiss()` implements **NearMiss-1** only: for each majority sample it averages the distances to its `k` *nearest* minority neighbors and keeps those with the smallest average (see `R/nearmiss_impl.R:88-90`). The docs cite Mani & Zhang (2003) but never state which of the three variants is used.

It would be nice to support all three variants from the original paper:

- **NearMiss-1** (implemented): keep majority samples with the smallest average distance to their `k` *nearest* minority neighbors.
- **NearMiss-2**: keep majority samples with the smallest average distance to their `k` *farthest* minority neighbors.
- **NearMiss-3**: two-step. First, for each minority sample keep its `M` nearest majority neighbors as a candidate pool; then from that pool keep the majority samples with the *largest* average distance to their `k` nearest minority neighbors.

### Notes on implementation

Most of the scaffolding is reusable (`downsample_count`, `subset_to_matrix`, `nn_dists_cross` with all distance metrics, the per-class loop).

- **NearMiss-2** is a small change: request all minority points as neighbors and average the `k` *largest* distances per row instead of the `k` smallest. The selection logic is otherwise identical.
- **NearMiss-3** needs an extra candidate-selection step using `$nn.idx`. It also does not naturally hit a fixed `under_ratio` target since the pool size is governed by `M`, so we need to decide how `under_ratio` interacts with it.

### Proposed API

Add a `version` argument to both `nearmiss()` and `step_nearmiss()` defaulting to `1` (preserving current behavior), and branch inside `nearmiss_impl()`, rather than adding three near-duplicate step functions.

References: Inderjeet Mani and I Zhang. kNN approach to unbalanced data distributions: a case study involving information extraction. In Proceedings of workshop on learning from imbalanced datasets, 2003.

title: Add replacement argument to step_downsample() for bootstrapped under-sampling
description:
## Current behavior

`step_downsample()` samples majority-class rows without replacement (the bake method notes "downsampling is done without replacement"), so each retained row is distinct.

## Proposal

Add a `replacement` argument (default `FALSE`) matching imbalanced-learn's `RandomUnderSampler`. With `replacement = TRUE` the under-sample is drawn with replacement (a bootstrapped under-sample), so the same row can be selected more than once. `FALSE` preserves the current behavior.

Implementation is passing `replace = replacement` to the sampling call in `bake.step_downsample()`.

## Notes

- `step_downsample()` supports case weights; with-replacement sampling composes naturally with weighted probabilities via `sample(prob = ...)`.
- Priority: low.

title: Add step_kmeans_smote() implementing KMeans-SMOTE over-sampling
description:
## Method

KMeans-SMOTE is an over-sampling method available in imbalanced-learn as `imblearn.over_sampling.KMeansSMOTE` that themis does not yet implement. It was identified while comparing themis's method coverage with imbalanced-learn.

It clusters the whole feature space, oversamples only inside clusters that are dominated by the minority class, and allocates more synthetic points to sparser clusters. This addresses SMOTE's main failure mode (generating noisy points in majority-dominated regions) and also counteracts within-class imbalance, not just between-class imbalance.

## Algorithm

Three stages:

1. Cluster the input space (imbalanced-learn uses `MiniBatchKMeans` by default).
2. Filter: keep a cluster only if the fraction of target-class points is at least `cluster_balance_threshold`. Clusters with too few minority points to run SMOTE are skipped.
3. Density-weighted SMOTE: for each kept cluster compute `sparsity = mean_pairwise_distance(minority)^exponent / n_points`, allocate `ceil(n_new * sparsity / sum(sparsity))` synthetic points per cluster, and generate them with ordinary SMOTE interpolation inside the cluster.

## Suggested API

Following the existing convention (a `step_*()` plus a direct-implementation counterpart):

- `step_kmeans_smote(recipe, ..., over_ratio = 1, neighbors = 2, num_clusters = NULL, cluster_balance_threshold = "auto", density_exponent = "auto", distance = "euclidean", seed, skip = TRUE)`
- `kmeans_smote(df, var, k = 2, over_ratio = 1, ...)`

Note that imbalanced-learn defaults `k_neighbors = 2` here, not 5 as in the other SMOTE variants.

Implementable with `stats::kmeans` (or an existing clustering dependency) plus the SMOTE machinery already in the package.

## Reference

Douzas, G., Bacao, F., & Last, F. (2018). Improving imbalanced learning through a heuristic oversampling method based on k-means and SMOTE. Information Sciences, 465, 1-20. (arXiv:1711.00837)

## Porting caveats

imbalanced-learn has two open correctness issues in its KMeansSMOTE that are worth avoiding by implementing from the paper rather than from their code:

- scikit-learn-contrib/imbalanced-learn#1186: divide-by-zero when all points in the valid clusters are identical (`cluster_sparsities.sum() == 0` produces `NaN`), and per-cluster `ceil` can overshoot the requested count.
- scikit-learn-contrib/imbalanced-learn#1050: the `cluster_balance_threshold = "auto"` formula includes a `/2` factor whose correctness is disputed; the original reference implementation defaulted this threshold to 1.0.

title: Add step_cluster_centroids() implementing ClusterCentroids prototype-generation under-sampling
description:
## Method

ClusterCentroids is an under-sampling method available in imbalanced-learn as `imblearn.under_sampling.ClusterCentroids` that themis does not yet implement. It was identified while comparing themis's method coverage with imbalanced-learn.

It is imbalanced-learn's only prototype-generation under-sampler, and themis currently has none: every existing under-sampling step (`step_downsample`, `step_nearmiss`, `step_tomek`, `step_cnn`, `step_enn`, `step_ncl`, `step_oss`, `step_instance_hardness`) selects existing rows. ClusterCentroids instead summarizes the majority class with cluster representatives, so adding it would fill that category.

## Algorithm

For each class being under-sampled, run k-means with `n_clusters` set to the target count for that class, then replace the class with:

- `voting = "soft"`: the centroid coordinates directly (synthetic points), or
- `voting = "hard"`: the nearest actual sample to each centroid (keeps real rows).

## Suggested API

Following the existing convention (a `step_*()` plus a direct-implementation counterpart):

- `step_cluster_centroids(recipe, ..., under_ratio = 1, voting = "soft", seed, skip = TRUE)`
- `cluster_centroids(df, var, under_ratio = 1, voting = "soft")`

Implementable with `stats::kmeans` plus RANN for the hard-voting nearest-sample lookup.

## Correctness note

Under hard voting the representative must be chosen from the target class only, not from all of `X`. This was a real bug in imbalanced-learn (scikit-learn-contrib/imbalanced-learn#769), worth getting right from the start.

## Reference

No canonical paper; imbalanced-learn documents it as generic cluster-centroid under-sampling.

title: Add kind_sel argument to step_enn() to support the stricter 'all' cleaning rule
description:
## Current behavior

`step_enn()` and `enn()` remove an observation when the mode of its nearest neighbors disagrees with its class. This is Wilson's original majority-vote ENN rule, implemented in `enn_single()` as `which(outcome != neighbor_mode)`.

## Proposal

Add a `kind_sel` argument matching imbalanced-learn's `EditedNearestNeighbours`, with two modes:

- `"mode"`: remove an observation if the majority (mode) of its neighbors disagree. This is themis's current behavior.
- `"all"`: remove an observation unless all of its neighbors share its class. Stricter, removes more.

imbalanced-learn defaults to `"all"`; themis currently only offers `"mode"`. Default `kind_sel = "mode"` in themis to preserve current behavior.

Implementation is a one-line branch in `enn_single()`: for `"all"`, flag a row when `any(neighbor_classes[i, ] != outcome[i])` instead of when the mode disagrees.

## Notes

- The change flows through to RENN and AllKNN automatically, since `times`/`all_k` reuse `enn_single()`.
- `step_ncl()`'s A1 stage corresponds to ENN with `kind_sel = "mode"` in imbalanced-learn; keep it on `"mode"` regardless of this argument.
- Priority: low.

title: step_svmsmote() hard-codes m, C, and kernel without exposing or documenting them
description:
## Problem

`step_svmsmote()` hard-codes several SVM/algorithm parameters that are neither exposed nor documented (around `R/svmsmote_impl.R:66` and `:181`):

- `m = 2 * k`
- `C = 1`
- kernel `rbfdot`

Users can't tune these, and the choices aren't documented, so behavior that depends on them is opaure.

## Suggested fix

Either expose these as arguments (with sensible defaults) or document the fixed choices and the rationale.

title: Consider using philentropy to expand available `distance` metrics
description:
## Summary

Investigate adding [philentropy](https://cran.r-project.org/package=philentropy) as a backend to broaden the set of distance metrics available to the nearest-neighbor-based steps (`step_cnn`, `step_tomek`, `step_oss`, `step_enn`, `step_nearmiss`, and the SMOTE family).

## Current state

Distance handling is centralized in three helpers in `R/misc.R`:

- `nn_indices()` — self kNN
- `nn_dists_cross()` / `nn_indices_cross()` — cross-set kNN

The supported metrics are fixed in `check_distance_arg()` (`R/misc.R:147`): `euclidean`, `cosine`, `mahalanobis`, `manhattan`, `chebyshev`. The first three use `RANN::nn2` (KD-tree) for fast NN lookup; `manhattan`/`chebyshev` fall back to a full O(n^2) `stats::dist()` matrix followed by `order`/`sort`.

## What philentropy adds

philentropy exposes ~46 distance/similarity measures, most notably the probability-distribution divergence family (Jensen-Shannon, KL divergence, Hellinger, Bhattacharyya, Canberra, Soergel, etc.), none of which themis currently offers. It's mature and well-cited with a single Rcpp dependency.

## Caveats

1. **No kNN indexing.** philentropy only computes distance *matrices*, so every philentropy metric would land on the existing slow O(n^2) path (same as the current manhattan/chebyshev fallback). It doesn't improve the fast RANN paths; RANN stays necessary for scale.
2. **Overlap.** euclidean, manhattan, chebyshev, and cosine are already covered. The genuinely new capability is the divergence measures.
3. **Semantics.** The divergence metrics assume each row is a probability distribution (non-negative, sums to one). Applying them to arbitrary standardized predictors is defined but often not meaningful, so it would need documentation guardrails.
4. Adds a new `Imports` dependency for a relatively niche feature.

## Proposed approach

Rather than swapping out the engine, scope it narrowly:

- Keep RANN for the existing fast metrics.
- Add a generic philentropy fallback branch in the three `nn_*` helpers, so any philentropy-supported method name flows through the existing `as.matrix(...)` -> `order`/`sort` path.
- Widen `check_distance_arg()` accordingly.

This is a small, localized change (three functions plus the validator), adds no slow path beyond what already exists, and unlocks the divergence family.

title: Add a methods-overview/taxonomy page (over/under with prototype selection vs generation, combination, regression)
description:
## Background

themis now has around 17 steps but no single page that explains how they relate to each other or how to choose between them. imbalanced-learn organizes its methods into a clear taxonomy, and adopting the same framing would help users navigate the package and would give new methods an obvious home.

## Proposed taxonomy

- Over-sampling (synthesize or replicate minority observations)
  - Random replication: `step_upsample()`
  - SMOTE family: `step_smote()`, `step_bsmote()`, `step_svmsmote()`, `step_smotenc()` (mixed types), `step_smoten()` (nominal), and `step_kmeans_smote()` once added (#317)
  - Adaptive: `step_adasyn()`
  - Smoothed bootstrap: `step_rose()`
- Under-sampling (reduce majority observations), split the way the imbalanced-learn maintainers think about it:
  - Prototype selection (keep a subset of the real rows)
    - Random: `step_downsample()`
    - Distance / near-boundary: `step_nearmiss()`, `step_tomek()`, `step_cnn()`, `step_oss()`
    - Neighborhood cleaning: `step_enn()` (with RENN and AllKNN via `times`/`all_k`), `step_ncl()`
    - Hardness: `step_instance_hardness()`
  - Prototype generation (create new representatives rather than keep real rows): currently none; `step_cluster_centroids()` once added (#318) would be the first
- Combination via composition (over-sample then clean): `step_smote() |> step_enn()`, `step_smote() |> step_tomek()` (#319)
- Regression (resample a numeric outcome): `step_smogn()`

The prototype selection vs prototype generation distinction is the useful one to surface: every current under-sampler selects existing rows, so ClusterCentroids fills a genuinely empty category.

## Proposed change

- A methods-overview article (vignette or article) presenting the taxonomy above with one line per method and guidance on when to reach for over- vs under- vs combination vs regression approaches.
- Consider mirroring the taxonomy in the `_pkgdown.yml` reference index, which currently groups only into Over-sampling, Under-sampling, and Methods.
- Add the new article to `_pkgdown.yml` and verify with `pkgdown::check_pkgdown()`.

## Notes

Pairs naturally with the README refresh and the common-pitfalls article.

title: Document SMOTE + ENN / SMOTE + Tomek composition as the equivalent of imbalanced-learn's combination samplers
description:
## Background

imbalanced-learn ships two combination methods in `imblearn.combine`: `SMOTEENN` (SMOTE then Edited Nearest Neighbours cleaning) and `SMOTETomek` (SMOTE then Tomek-link removal). Both over-sample the minority class and then run a cleaning under-sampler on the combined real-plus-synthetic data to remove the ambiguous points SMOTE tends to create near the class boundary.

imbalanced-learn ships these as single objects mainly because a scikit-learn pipeline cannot chain two samplers around one estimator. Recipes has no such limitation: the idiomatic equivalents are already expressible today as

```r
recipe(...) |> step_smote(class) |> step_enn(class)
recipe(...) |> step_smote(class) |> step_tomek(class)
```

So this is a documentation gap, not a missing feature.

## Why the composition already matches

`step_enn()` cleans all classes: `enn_single()` flags every row where the class differs from the mode of its neighbors, including freshly synthesized minority points. That is exactly what imbalanced-learn's `SMOTEENN` configures via `sampling_strategy = "all"` on its ENN step, so `step_smote() |> step_enn()` reproduces SMOTEENN semantics closely rather than approximately.

One subtlety worth mentioning in the docs: standalone imbalanced-learn `EditedNearestNeighbours` defaults to cleaning "not minority", whereas themis's `step_enn()` cleans every class. This means themis's step is already tuned toward the combined (post-SMOTE) use case.

## Proposed change

Document the composition pattern rather than add wrapper steps. Options:

- A short section in a vignette or article showing SMOTE + ENN and SMOTE + Tomek, with a note on ordering (over-sample first, then clean) and on the all-class cleaning behavior above.
- A "see also" cross-reference between `step_smote()`, `step_enn()`, and `step_tomek()` pointing at that section.

If wrapper steps such as `step_smoteenn()` are ever desired for discoverability, they would be thin compositions, and the only behavior to pin down is the class scope of the cleaning stage.

title: Add a 'common pitfalls' article: resample the training set only (skip = TRUE) and avoid CV leakage
description:
## Background

imbalanced-learn has an excellent [Common pitfalls and recommended practices](https://imbalanced-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html) page. Its core message maps directly onto themis, and we should have an equivalent article, especially for users migrating from Python who will look for it.

The key idea: resampling must only ever touch the training data, never the data you evaluate on, and resampling before the cross-validation split is data leakage that produces inflated, unrealistic performance estimates. imbalanced-learn's entire `Pipeline` design exists to enforce this (a sampler's `fit_resample` runs during `fit` on the training fold only, and is bypassed at `predict`/`score`). themis gets the same guarantee for free through recipes and workflows via `skip = TRUE`, and the docs should say so explicitly rather than leave it implicit.

## Proposed article outline

1. Resample the training set only. All row-changing themis steps default to `skip = TRUE`, so they run at `prep()` and at `bake(new_data = NULL)` (training) but are skipped when a workflow bakes new data at `predict()` time. The assessment/test set keeps its natural class balance. Show what `skip = TRUE` does and why the default is what you want.
2. Do not resample before splitting or before cross-validation. Applying a sampling step to the whole data set before `initial_split()` or `vfold_cv()` leaks duplicated or synthetic points across folds. The correct pattern is to put the step in a recipe inside a workflow and let `fit_resample()`/`tune_grid()` apply it inside each analysis fold only.
3. Evaluate on the natural distribution. Because the step is skipped on the assessment set, metrics are computed on the real class balance, which is the honest estimate.
4. The imbalanced-learn parallel. A short note that recipes `skip = TRUE` plus workflows is the structural equivalent of imbalanced-learn's `Pipeline` "resample train, bypass test" behavior.

A worked example contrasting the leaky approach (resample then cross-validate) with the correct approach (cross-validate a workflow containing the recipe), showing the gap in estimated performance, would mirror the imbalanced-learn page well.

## Notes

- This pairs naturally with the taxonomy/overview and README-refresh documentation work.
- Add the new article to `_pkgdown.yml` and check with `pkgdown::check_pkgdown()`.

## Problem

`smoten_impl()` makes two VDM design choices that are defensible but deviate from Chawla's stated form and aren't documented:

- VDM aggregates per-feature deltas with r = 1 (sum) rather than r = 2 (Euclidean).

title: Document multiclass semantics of step_nearmiss() and step_oss()
description:
## Problem

Some multiclass behaviors are undocumented and differ from common references:

- **NearMiss** measures distance to all other classes, not just the minority (imbalanced-learn measures to the minority). 
- **Multiclass OSS** would remove both members of majority-majority Tomek links.

The binary case (the primary, documented use) is correct; the multiclass semantics are simply not spelled out, which can surprise users applying these steps to >2 classes.

## Suggested fix

Document the multiclass behavior of `step_nearmiss()` and `step_oss()` (and note where it differs from imbalanced-learn), or constrain/align it if a specific semantics is intended.

title: Lean into themis's strengths in the intro: regression resampling and multiple distance metrics
description:
## Background

themis has two capabilities that are uncommon among resampling tools but are easy to miss from the current README and pkgdown landing page, which are framed almost entirely around classification with default Euclidean distance. A sentence or two up front would help users understand the breadth of the package and find these features.

## The two strengths to surface

1. Regression resampling. `step_smogn()` resamples an imbalanced numeric outcome (over-sampling rare regions and under-sampling common ones), so themis is not limited to classification imbalance.
2. Multiple distance metrics. The nearest-neighbor-based steps accept a `distance` argument supporting euclidean, cosine, mahalanobis, manhattan, and chebyshev, rather than assuming Euclidean.

## Proposed change

- Add a short intro paragraph (README and the pkgdown home or getting-started page) noting that themis handles both classification and regression imbalance and that its distance-based steps support several metrics.
- Keep it to a couple of sentences; the goal is discoverability, not a feature dump.

## Notes

Pairs naturally with the README refresh and the methods-overview/taxonomy page.

title: step_upsample() bootstraps classes above target when over_ratio < 1; indicator_column changes output
description:
## Problem

Two related defects in `step_upsample()` (`R/upsample.R`, `supsamp()` around lines 244-256 vs `supsamp_with_indicator()` around 258-271):

1. **Classes above target get bootstrapped instead of left alone.** `supsamp()` does
   ```r
   sample(seq_len(n), max(num, n), replace = TRUE, prob = wts)
   ```
   When a class already exceeds the target (`n > num`), `max(num, n) == n`, so it resamples the class to its own size *with replacement*: some rows duplicated, some dropped, count unchanged. The docs (around `R/upsample.R:101-102`) promise such classes "are left alone". This bites any `over_ratio < 1`, and multiclass sets with intermediate class sizes.
2. **`indicator_column` changes which rows are produced.** The non-indicator path full-bootstraps, while `supsamp_with_indicator()` keeps all originals and appends duplicates. So toggling `indicator_column` changes the output for the same seed.

## Reproducing

```r
# class with n = 100, target num = 50 (over_ratio = 0.5)
# count stays 100 but only ~52 distinct originals survive
# and the indicator vs non-indicator path keep different rows for the same seed
```

## Suggested fix

Early-return untouched classes in `supsamp()` (`if (n >= num) return(x)`) and make it keep originals + append duplicates, so both paths agree.

title: `distance = "mahalanobis"` uses the wrong Cholesky factor
description:
**Severity:** high · **Status:** CONFIRMED · **Files:** `R/misc.R:176,210-213,249-252`; `R/smogn_impl.R:220`

All four sites whiten with `m %*% solve(t(chol(S)))`. With `S = RᵀR` (`chol` returns upper `R`), this gives `W = R⁻ᵀ`, so `WWᵀ = (RRᵀ)⁻¹ ≠ Σ⁻¹`. The correct whitening is `m %*% solve(chol(S))` (`W = R⁻¹` → `WWᵀ = Σ⁻¹`).

Reproduction on correlated data: `max|themis − true Mahalanobis| ≈ 58` (200×4); the corrected form matches `stats::mahalanobis` to ~1e-15; and the returned **nearest-neighbor sets differ** (true 5-NN `{114,191,68,58,72}` vs themis `{114,72,191,124,68}`). So this corrupts *index* consumers (who interpolates with whom, who is removed), not just distance magnitudes. It is only near-correct when the covariance is near-diagonal, i.e. exactly the case where Mahalanobis is unnecessary. Reachable via every step that offers `distance`, and independently inside SMOGN.

**Suggested fix:** `solve(chol(S))` at all four sites (ideally fix once via deduplication).

title: Borderline-SMOTE selects the wrong points ("danger" set is inverted)
description:
**Severity:** critical · **Status:** CONFIRMED · **Files:** `R/bsmote_impl.R:88-91,130-132`

`x` is the count of **minority** neighbors (`min_class_in <- df[[var]] == min_names[i]`, summed over neighbors, minus self), but `danger(x, k) <- (x != k) & (k/2 <= x)` is written as if `x` were the **majority** count. Han (2005) defines danger as `k/2 <= (majority neighbors) < k`, i.e. `0 < x <= k/2`.

Reproduction (truth table at `k = 5`):

| x (minority nbrs) | majority nbrs | themis danger | Han danger |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4 | FALSE | **TRUE** |
| 2 | 3 | FALSE | **TRUE** |
| 3 | 2 | **TRUE** | FALSE |
| 4 | 1 | **TRUE** | FALSE |

themis's danger set is the **safe** set and vice versa: the two are disjoint. The noise exclusion `x != k` also excludes all-minority points instead of the all-majority noise points. Net effect: BSMOTE oversamples safe interior points, defeating the algorithm's purpose. Affects both `all_neighbors = FALSE/TRUE`.

**Suggested fix:** compute the majority-neighbor count (or use `x > 0 & x <= k/2`), and exclude `x == 0` (all-majority) as noise.

title: NearMiss keeps the wrong rows (`order()` used where `rank()` is required)
description:
**Severity:** high · **Status:** CONFIRMED · **Files:** `R/nearmiss_impl.R:90`

`selected_ind <- order(rowMeans(dists)) <= (nrow(class) - classes[i])`. `order(v) <= n` is a positional predicate, not "the n smallest" (that is `rank(v) <= n`).

Reproduction: minority near 0, majority at `{10, 1, 11, 2, 3}`, `under_ratio = 1` keeps `{2, 3, 10}` when NearMiss-1 must keep the three closest `{1, 2, 3}`; it drops the nearest point and keeps a far one. Kept *count* is right, kept *rows* are wrong. Metric-independent (active on the default euclidean).

**Suggested fix:** `rank(rowMeans(dists), ties.method = "first") <= (nrow(class) - classes[i])`. The sibling `instance_hardness_impl.R:108` already does exactly this.

title: Unused outcome factor level silently deletes all rows at `prep()`
description:
**Severity:** high · **Status:** CONFIRMED · **Files:** `R/downsample.R:211,221`; `R/nearmiss_impl.R:103-108`; `R/instance_hardness_impl.R:75,107`

These derive the target from `min(table(outcome))`, which counts empty levels as 0, and none call `droplevels()`, so `target = 0` and every class is sampled to 0 rows. `prep()` bakes the training data even with `skip = TRUE`, so this fires on an ordinary `prep()`.

Reproduction: adding one unused level to `circle_example$class` makes `step_downsample`, `step_nearmiss`, and `step_instance_hardness` each return **0 rows** (`step_upsample` survives). Unused levels are common after filtering.

**Suggested fix:** `droplevels()` the outcome (or skip zero-count levels) before computing targets.

title: SVM SMOTE
description:
## Feature Request

Add support for SVM SMOTE (Support Vector Machine SMOTE).

## Description

SVM SMOTE is a variant of SMOTE that uses Support Vector Machine to identify the decision boundary. Instead of using k-nearest neighbors to find where to generate synthetic samples, it:

1. Fits an SVM model to the data
2. Identifies the support vectors from the minority classes
3. Generates synthetic observations around those support vectors

This focuses synthetic sample generation on the decision boundary where it matters most for classification.

## References

- Nguyen, H. M., Cooper, E. W., & Kamei, K. (2011). Borderline over-sampling for imbalanced data classification. International Journal of Knowledge Engineering and Soft Data Paradigms, 3(1), 4-21.

title: Add SMOTEN
description:
## Feature Request

Add support for SMOTEN (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique for Nominal data).

## Description

SMOTEN is a variant of SMOTE designed specifically for categorical (nominal) data. Since standard SMOTE relies on interpolation between points in continuous space, it cannot be directly applied to categorical features.

## Algorithm

1. Use Value Difference Metric (VDM) instead of Euclidean distance to calculate distances between categorical observations
2. For each minority class sample, find k-nearest neighbors using VDM
3. Generate synthetic samples by selecting the most frequent category for each feature among the sample and its selected neighbor

## Key Properties

- Works with purely categorical data
- Uses Value Difference Metric for neighbor calculation
- Generated samples use existing category values (no interpolation)
- May generate implausible combinations of categories

## Relationship to Other Methods

- Variant of: SMOTE (`step_smote()`)
- Related: SMOTENC (handles mixed numeric and categorical data)

## References

- Chawla, N. V., Bowyer, K. W., Hall, L. O., & Kegelmeyer, W. P. (2002). SMOTE: synthetic minority over-sampling technique. Journal of artificial intelligence research, 16, 321-357.
- https://imbalanced-learn.org/stable/references/generated/imblearn.over_sampling.SMOTEN.html

title: add SMOGN
description:
## Feature Request

Add support for SMOGN (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique for Regression with Gaussian Noise).

## Description

SMOGN extends SMOTE-based approaches to regression problems. While SMOTE and its variants are designed for classification with discrete class labels, SMOGN handles continuous target variables by identifying "rare" regions in the target distribution.

## Algorithm

1. Identify rare/extreme values in the continuous target variable using a relevance function
2. For samples in rare regions:
   - Find k-nearest neighbors
   - Generate synthetic samples by interpolating between neighbors
   - Add Gaussian noise to prevent overfitting
3. Optionally under-sample common regions

## Key Properties

- Extends SMOTE concepts to regression tasks
- Uses relevance function to identify what constitutes "rare" values
- Adds Gaussian noise to synthetic samples for regularization
- Can combine over-sampling of rare regions with under-sampling of common regions

## Relationship to Other Methods

- Extends: SMOTE concepts to regression
- Related: SMOTE (`step_smote()`)

## References

- Branco, P., Torgo, L., & Ribeiro, R. P. (2017). SMOGN: a pre-processing approach for imbalanced regression. In First International Workshop on Learning with Imbalanced Domains: Theory and Applications (pp. 36-50). PMLR.
- http://proceedings.mlr.press/v74/branco17a/branco17a.pdf

title: One-sided Selection
description:
## Feature Request

Add support for One-Sided Selection (OSS) under-sampling.

## Description

One-Sided Selection is an under-sampling technique that combines Tomek Links and Condensed Nearest Neighbor (CNN) to clean and reduce the majority class.

## Algorithm

1. Apply Tomek Links removal to eliminate majority class samples that form Tomek links with minority class samples (boundary cleaning)
2. Apply Condensed Nearest Neighbor to further reduce the majority class while preserving samples needed for classification

This two-stage approach first removes noisy/borderline majority samples, then reduces redundant majority samples.

## Relationship to Other Methods

- Uses: Tomek Links (already implemented as `step_tomek()`)
- Uses: Condensed Nearest Neighbor (#113)

## References

- Kubat, M., & Matwin, S. (1997). Addressing the curse of imbalanced training sets: one-sided selection. In ICML (Vol. 97, pp. 179-186).
- https://imbalanced-learn.org/stable/references/generated/imblearn.under_sampling.OneSidedSelection.html

title: Condensed Nearest Neighbor
description:
## Feature Request

Add support for Condensed Nearest Neighbor (CNN) under-sampling.

## Description

Condensed Nearest Neighbor is a data reduction technique that selects a subset of the majority class while preserving classification accuracy. It aims to keep only the samples necessary for correctly classifying all original training points using a 1-NN classifier.

## Algorithm

1. Initialize a "store" set with all minority class samples and one random sample from the majority class
2. Train a 1-Nearest Neighbor classifier on the store
3. For each remaining majority class sample:
   - If it is misclassified by the 1-NN using the current store, add it to the store
4. Repeat steps 2-3 until no new samples are added

The result is a reduced dataset that keeps boundary points and discards redundant interior points.

## Key Properties

- Reduces dataset size significantly for well-separated classes
- Preserves decision boundaries
- Order-dependent (results can vary based on processing order)
- Sensitive to noise (noisy points often get included)

## References

- Hart, P. (1968). The condensed nearest neighbor rule. IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 14(3), 515-516.
- https://imbalanced-learn.org/stable/references/generated/imblearn.under_sampling.CondensedNearestNeighbour.html

title: Neighborhood Cleaning Rule
description:
## Feature Request

Add support for Neighborhood Cleaning Rule (NCL) under-sampling.

## Description

Neighborhood Cleaning Rule is an under-sampling technique that focuses on cleaning the data by removing majority class samples that are noisy or that cause minority class samples to be misclassified.

## Algorithm

1. Apply Edited Nearest Neighbor (ENN) to remove majority class samples misclassified by their neighbors
2. For each minority class sample:
   - Find its k-nearest neighbors
   - If the majority of neighbors are from the majority class, remove those majority class neighbors

This method is more focused on cleaning around minority class samples than standard ENN.

## Key Properties

- Focuses on cleaning around minority class samples
- Removes majority samples that "pollute" minority class neighborhoods
- Less aggressive than pure ENN on majority class overall

## Relationship to Other Methods

- Based on: Edited Nearest Neighbor (#115)
- Related: Repeated Edited Nearest Neighbor (#173)
- Related: AllKNN (#174)

## References

- Laurikkala, J. (2001). Improving identification of difficult small classes by balancing class distribution. In Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Medicine in Europe (pp. 63-66). Springer.
- https://imbalanced-learn.org/stable/references/generated/imblearn.under_sampling.NeighbourhoodCleaningRule.html

title: Add algorithm details pages to both implementation and step functions
description:
Each sampling method in themis is exposed through two functions: an implementation function (e.g. `smote()`) and a recipes step (e.g. `step_smote()`). We should make sure both function's documentation includes a details section describing the underlying algorithm itself.

The goal is that a user reading either the `smote()` help page or the `step_smote()` help page gets an explanation of how the algorithm works, rather than having to hunt for it in only one of the two places.

This applies to all method pairs, including:

- `smote()` / `step_smote()`
- `bsmote()` / `step_bsmote()`
- `adasyn()` / `step_adasyn()`
- `nearmiss()` / `step_nearmiss()`
- `tomek()` / `step_tomek()`
- `enn()` / `step_enn()`
- `smotenc()` / `step_smotenc()`
- and any other implementation/step pairs

We could either duplicate the description or use a shared `@includeRmd`/roxygen template so the algorithm description stays in sync between the two pages.

title: AllKNN
description:
## Feature Request

Add support for AllKNN under-sampling.

## Description

AllKNN is a variant of Edited Nearest Neighbor (ENN) that iteratively applies ENN with increasing values of k.

## Algorithm

1. For k = 1 to some maximum K:
   - Apply ENN with the current k value
   - Remove samples where the majority of k neighbors belong to a different class
2. The final dataset is the result after all iterations

This is more thorough than standard ENN as it considers neighborhood relationships at multiple scales.

## Relationship to Other Methods

- Extends: Edited Nearest Neighbor (#115)
- Related: Repeated Edited Nearest Neighbor (see separate issue)

## References

- Tomek, I. (1976). Two modifications of CNN. IEEE Trans. Systems, Man and Cybernetics, 6, 769-772.

title: Repeated Edited Nearest Neighbor
description:
## Feature Request

Add support for Repeated Edited Nearest Neighbor (RENN) under-sampling.

## Description

Repeated Edited Nearest Neighbor is an extension of Edited Nearest Neighbor (ENN) that applies the ENN algorithm iteratively until no more samples are removed.

## Algorithm

1. Apply ENN: For each sample, if the majority of its k-nearest neighbors belong to a different class, remove it
2. Repeat step 1 until no more samples are removed (convergence)

This results in more aggressive cleaning than single-pass ENN, removing more noisy and borderline samples.

## Relationship to Other Methods

- Extends: Edited Nearest Neighbor (#115)
- Related: AllKNN (see separate issue)

## References

- Tomek, I. (1976). An experiment with the edited nearest-neighbor rule. IEEE Transactions on systems, Man, and Cybernetics, (6), 448-452.

title: Edited Nearest Neighbor
description:
## Feature Request

Add support for Edited Nearest Neighbor (ENN) under-sampling.

## Description

Edited Nearest Neighbor is an under-sampling technique that removes samples whose class label differs from the majority of their k-nearest neighbors. This effectively removes noisy and borderline samples.

## Algorithm

1. For each sample in the dataset:
   - Find its k-nearest neighbors
   - If the majority of neighbors belong to a different class, mark the sample for removal
2. Remove all marked samples

This is a cleaning method that removes misclassified or ambiguous samples, resulting in smoother decision boundaries.

## Key Properties

- Removes noisy samples that are likely misclassified
- Cleans decision boundaries
- Can be applied to majority class only, or to all classes
- Often used as a preprocessing step before other methods

## Relationship to Other Methods

- Extended by: Repeated Edited Nearest Neighbor (#173)
- Extended by: AllKNN (#174)
- Related: Neighborhood Cleaning Rule (#116)

## References

- Wilson, D. L. (1972). Asymptotic properties of nearest neighbor rules using edited data. IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, (3), 408-421.
- https://imbalanced-learn.org/stable/references/generated/imblearn.under_sampling.EditedNearestNeighbours.html

title: Instance Hardness Threshold
description:
## Feature Request

Add support for Instance Hardness Threshold under-sampling.

## Description

Instance Hardness Threshold is an under-sampling technique that removes samples from the majority class based on how "hard" they are to classify.

## Algorithm

1. Train a classifier (typically cross-validated) on the dataset
2. For each sample, compute its "hardness" - the probability of misclassification
3. Remove majority class samples that have hardness below a threshold (i.e., samples that are easy to classify and thus potentially redundant)

The intuition is that easy-to-classify majority samples are less informative for learning the decision boundary, so removing them balances the dataset while preserving the most informative samples.

## References

- Smith, M. R., Martinez, T., & Giraud-Carrier, C. (2014). An instance level analysis of data complexity. Machine learning, 95(2), 225-256.

title: SMOTE distance metric variants
description:
## Feature Request

Add support for SMOTE variants using alternative distance metrics.

## Description

The standard SMOTE algorithm uses Euclidean distance for nearest neighbor calculations. However, alternative distance metrics can be more appropriate depending on the data characteristics. This issue proposes adding support for:

- **SMOTE-Cosine**: Uses cosine distance, useful when the direction of the feature vector matters more than magnitude
- **SMOTE-Mahalanobis**: Uses Mahalanobis distance, accounts for correlations between features
- **SMOTE-Manhattan**: Uses Manhattan (L1) distance, can be more robust to outliers
- **SMOTE-Chebyshev**: Uses Chebyshev (L∞) distance, considers maximum difference across dimensions

## Implementation

This could be implemented as a `distance` argument to `step_smote()` (and potentially `step_bsmote()` and `step_adasyn()`), e.g.:

```r
step_smote(class, distance = "euclidean")
step_smote(class, distance = "cosine")
step_smote(class, distance = "mahalanobis")
step_smote(class, distance = "manhattan")
step_smote(class, distance = "chebyshev")
```

title: Add a vignette introducing the package and helping users choose between methods
description:
## Issue

The package currently has no vignettes. Users have only per-function reference documentation, with no narrative guide to help them:

- Understand the difference between over-sampling and under-sampling
- Choose between SMOTE, BSMOTE, ADASYN, SMOTENC, ROSE, upsample
- Choose between NearMiss, Tomek, downsample
- Understand why `skip = TRUE` matters and how it interacts with resampling workflows
- Integrate a sampling step correctly into a full tidymodels pipeline (with `tune`, `workflow`, `fit_resamples`, etc.)
- Understand `over_ratio` and `under_ratio` intuitively

For a package with 9 distinct algorithms, the absence of a vignette is a significant gap in discoverability and usability.

## Suggested content for a first vignette

A single vignette covering the basics would go a long way:

1. Motivation — what does class imbalance mean and why does it matter?
2. The `circle_example` dataset as a visual introduction
3. Over-sampling vs under-sampling — when to use which
4. A quick tour of the steps with `circle_example` plots showing what each method does geometrically
5. A complete tidymodels workflow example using `workflow` + `tune_grid` with `skip = TRUE` explained
6. Guidance on `over_ratio` / `under_ratio`

A second vignette on SMOTENC (the only step that handles mixed data) would also be valuable given its unique capabilities and more complex setup.

title: No standalone rose() function, unlike every other algorithm in the package
description:
## Issue

Every algorithm in themis that has a recipe step also exports a standalone function for direct use:

| Algorithm | Step | Standalone |
|-----------|------|------------|
| SMOTE | `step_smote()` | `smote()` ✓ |
| BSMOTE | `step_bsmote()` | `bsmote()` ✓ |
| ADASYN | `step_adasyn()` | `adasyn()` ✓ |
| SMOTENC | `step_smotenc()` | `smotenc()` ✓ |
| NearMiss | `step_nearmiss()` | `nearmiss()` ✓ |
| Tomek | `step_tomek()` | `tomek()` ✓ |
| ROSE | `step_rose()` | — ✗ |
| Upsample | `step_upsample()` | — (simple, intentional) |
| Downsample | `step_downsample()` | — (simple, intentional) |

ROSE is the only non-trivial algorithm without a standalone function. Users who want to apply ROSE outside of a recipe have no themis-provided interface to do so — they must call `ROSE::ROSE()` directly, which requires understanding its formula interface and parameters.

## Suggested fix

Add an exported `rose()` function in `R/rose.R` following the same pattern as the other standalone functions:

```r
rose <- function(df, var, over_ratio = 1, minority_prop = 0.5,
                 minority_smoothness = 1, majority_smoothness = 1) {
  # validate inputs
  # call ROSE::ROSE() directly
}
```

This would also make `rose` consistent with the other entries in the "Methods" section of the pkgdown reference.

title: adasyn() standalone function cites the wrong reference (SMOTE instead of ADASYN)
description:
## Bug

The documentation for the standalone `adasyn()` function in `R/adasyn_impl.R` cites the SMOTE paper (Chawla et al. 2002) instead of the ADASYN paper (He et al. 2008). The correct reference is present in `step_adasyn()` but was not carried over to the standalone function.

## Current (incorrect) reference in `adasyn()` docs

```r
#' @references Chawla, N. V., Bowyer, K. W., Hall, L. O., and Kegelmeyer,
#'  W. P. (2002). Smote: Synthetic minority over-sampling technique.
#'  Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, 16:321-357.
```

## Correct reference (from `step_adasyn()`)

```r
#' @references He, H., Bai, Y., Garcia, E. and Li, S. 2008. ADASYN: Adaptive
#'  synthetic sampling approach for imbalanced learning. Proceedings of
#'  IJCNN 2008. (IEEE World Congress on Computational Intelligence). IEEE
#'  International Joint Conference. pp.1322-1328.
```

## Fix

Replace the `@references` tag in `R/adasyn_impl.R` with the correct ADASYN citation, then re-document.

title: over_ratio parameter documentation has grammar error ('than' should be 'as')
description:
## Issue

The `over_ratio` parameter documentation inherited by all over-sampling steps from `step_upsample()` contains a grammar error:

> A value of 0.5 would mean that the minority levels will have (at most) (approximately) half as many rows **than** the majority level.

"Half as many rows than" is ungrammatical. It should be "half as many rows **as** the majority level."

## Affected steps

All steps that use `@inheritParams step_upsample` for `over_ratio`: `step_smote`, `step_bsmote`, `step_adasyn`, `step_smotenc`, `step_rose`. The fix is in the `over_ratio` parameter documentation in `R/upsample.R`, from which all others inherit.

## Fix

In `R/upsample.R`, change:

```r
#' @param over_ratio A numeric value for the ratio of the
#'  minority-to-majority frequencies. The default value (1) means
#'  that all other levels are sampled up to have the same
#'  frequency as the most occurring level. A value of 0.5 would mean
#'  that the minority levels will have (at most) (approximately)
#'  half as many rows than the majority level.
```

to:

```r
#' @param over_ratio A numeric value for the ratio of the
#'  minority-to-majority frequencies. The default value (1) means
#'  that all other levels are sampled up to have the same
#'  frequency as the most occurring level. A value of 0.5 would mean
#'  that the minority levels will have (at most) (approximately)
#'  half as many rows as the majority level.
```

title: nearmiss_impl() error message uses bsmote-specific 'danger observations' terminology
description:
## Issue

`nearmiss_impl()` in `R/nearmiss_impl.R` produces a confusing error message that borrows terminology from the BSMOTE algorithm:

```r
cli::cli_abort(
  "Not enough danger observations of {.val {names(classes)[i]}} to perform NEARMISS."
)
```

"Danger observations" is specific to BSMOTE, where points are classified into "danger" and "safe" zones. It has no meaning in the context of NearMiss, which is a distance-based undersampling algorithm. A user hitting this error would find the message confusing and potentially misleading.

## Fix

Replace with a message appropriate to NearMiss, e.g.:

```r
cli::cli_abort(
  "Not enough observations in the other classes to compute {k} nearest neighbors \\
  for {.val {names(classes)[i]}}."
)
```

title: step_tomek() documentation incorrectly states it requires exactly 2 class levels
description:
## Issue

The documentation for `step_tomek()` states:

> The factor variable used to balance around must only have 2 levels.

This is incorrect. `tomek_impl()` loops over `unique(outcome)` and works correctly with any number of classes. The `check_2_levels_only()` guard (used by `step_rose()`) is not called in `step_tomek()`, and multi-class usage works fine in practice.

## Evidence

```r
library(recipes)
library(themis)
library(modeldata)

# 3-class dataset — works fine despite the docs saying it shouldn't
recipe(species ~ bill_length_mm + bill_depth_mm, data = penguins) |>
  step_impute_mean(all_predictors()) |>
  step_tomek(species) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  count(species)
```

## Fix

Update the `@details` section in `R/tomek.R` to reflect that multi-class data is supported. The incorrect sentence is:

> The factor variable used to balance around must only have 2 levels. All other variables must be numerics with no missing data.

It should say something like:

> All variables other than the class variable must be numeric with no missing data.

title: Error when running `step_bsmote` with a single predictor
description:
## The problem

When running `step_bsmote()` with only a single predictor, the function throws an error that a matrix cannot be created. This is due to `themis:::bsmote_impl()` at line 19: the `data` argument for `smote_data()` is given by subsetting `data_mat` with the values of `min_class_in`, but due to how the pesky subset `[` works, the matrix is simplified to a vector in the case of only a single column. Thus, running `step_bsmote()` with a single predictor always throws this error.  

The fix is by specifying `drop = FALSE` when subsetting `data_mat`, so that line 19 becomes:

```r
tmp_df <- as.data.frame(smote_data(data = data_mat[min_class_in, , drop = FALSE], k = k, n_samples = samples_needed[i], smote_ids = which(danger_ids[min_class_in])))
```

## Reproducible example

``` r
library(tidymodels)
library(themis)

recipe(class ~ compounds, data = hpc_data) |> 
  step_bsmote(all_outcomes(), all_neighbors = FALSE) |> 
  prep() |> 
  bake(NULL)
#> Error in `step_bsmote()`:
#> Caused by error in `matrix()`:
#> ! non-numeric matrix extent
```

suppressWarnings() around gower::gower_topn() in smotenc_impl() hides real warnings
description:
## Issue

In `R/smotenc_impl.R`, the call to `gower::gower_topn()` is wrapped in `suppressWarnings()`, which blindly suppresses all warnings from that call. If gower emits a meaningful warning (e.g. about column type mismatches or unsupported types), it will be silently swallowed and users will have no indication something is wrong.

## Current code

```r
suppressWarnings(
  ids <- t(
    gower::gower_topn(x = data, y = data, n = k + 1, nthread = 1)$index
  )
)
```

## Investigation needed

Before removing the suppression it is worth checking:
1. What warning(s) does `gower::gower_topn()` emit that prompted this suppression?
2. Are those warnings expected/harmless in this context?

If the warnings are known and benign (e.g. a specific deprecation or a known gower behaviour for certain column types), they should be suppressed selectively using `withCallingHandlers()` matching only those specific warning classes, rather than suppressing everything.

If the original reason for `suppressWarnings()` is no longer applicable (e.g. a gower version bump fixed the issue), the suppression should simply be removed.

Replace deprecated purrr::map2_dfr() in step_upsample() and step_downsample()
description:
## Issue

`bake.step_upsample()` and `bake.step_downsample()` both use `purrr::map2_dfr()`, which was deprecated in purrr 1.0.0 (2022). Users on modern purrr installations will see deprecation warnings when baking these steps.

The `themis-package.R` file also has `@importFrom purrr map_dfr` which is similarly deprecated.

## Affected code

```r
# R/upsample.R — bake.step_upsample()
new_data <- purrr::map2_dfr(
  split_data,
  split_wts,
  supsamp,
  num = object$target
)

# R/downsample.R — bake.step_downsample()
new_data <- purrr::map2_dfr(
  split_data,
  split_wts,
  subsamp,
  num = object$target
)
```

## Fix

Replace with the modern equivalent:

```r
new_data <- purrr::map2(split_data, split_wts, supsamp, num = object$target) |>
  list_rbind()
```

Also remove `@importFrom purrr map_dfr` from `R/themis-package.R` if it is no longer used after this change.

title: get_from_info() na_rm argument is never used and can be removed
description:
## Issue

`get_from_info()` in `R/misc.R` exposes a `na_rm` parameter that is never passed as anything other than its default (`TRUE`) anywhere in the package:

```r
get_from_info <- function(info, role, na_rm = TRUE) {
  res <- info$variable[info$role == role]
  if (na_rm) {
    res <- stats::na.omit(res)
  }
  res
}
```

Every call site in the package uses the default:

```r
predictors <- setdiff(get_from_info(info, "predictor"), col_name)
```

The `na_rm = FALSE` path is dead code — it has never been used internally and is not part of the public API (the function is not exported). The parameter adds surface area without providing any value.

## Fix

Remove the `na_rm` parameter and always apply `stats::na.omit()`:

```r
get_from_info <- function(info, role) {
  res <- info$variable[info$role == role]
  stats::na.omit(res)
}
```

bsmote(): all_neighbors argument is silently ignored
description:
## Bug

The standalone `bsmote()` function accepts an `all_neighbors` argument but never passes it to `bsmote_impl()`, so it is always silently ignored. The function always behaves as if `all_neighbors = FALSE` regardless of what the user specifies.

## Minimal example

```r
library(themis)
circle_numeric <- circle_example[, c("x", "y", "class")]

# These two calls should produce different results, but they produce identical output
res_false <- bsmote(circle_numeric, var = "class", all_neighbors = FALSE, seed = 1)
res_true  <- bsmote(circle_numeric, var = "class", all_neighbors = TRUE,  seed = 1)

identical(res_false, res_true)  # TRUE — bug
```

## Root cause

In `R/bsmote_impl.R`, the `bsmote()` wrapper validates `all_neighbors` but drops it on the call to `bsmote_impl()`:

```r
bsmote <- function(df, var, k = 5, over_ratio = 1, all_neighbors = FALSE) {
  # ... validation including check_bool(all_neighbors) ...
  bsmote_impl(df, var, k, over_ratio)  # all_neighbors never passed!
}
```

`bsmote_impl()` has the parameter: `bsmote_impl(df, var, k = 5, over_ratio = 1, all_neighbors = FALSE)`.

## Fix

```r
bsmote_impl(df, var, k, over_ratio, all_neighbors)
```

Note: the recipe step (`bake.step_bsmote`) correctly passes `all_neighbors` via `bsmote_impl(..., all_neighbors = object$all_neighbors)`, so this bug only affects direct use of the `bsmote()` function.

title: Duplicate id = id argument in step_*_new() constructors
description:
## Bug

Seven of the nine `step_*_new()` constructor functions pass the `id` argument twice to `recipes::step()`. R silently uses the last value, so this is not currently breaking, but it is a latent source of confusion and dead code.

## Affected files

- `R/smote.R` — `step_smote_new()`
- `R/bsmote.R` — `step_bsmote_new()`
- `R/adasyn.R` — `step_adasyn_new()`
- `R/nearmiss.R` — `step_nearmiss_new()`
- `R/smotenc.R` — `step_smotenc_new()`
- `R/tomek.R` — `step_tomek_new()`
- `R/downsample.R` — `step_downsample_new()`

## Example (from `R/smote.R`)

```r
step_smote_new <- function(terms, role, trained, column, over_ratio,
                            neighbors, predictors, skip, seed, id) {
  step(
    subclass = "smote",
    ...
    skip = skip,
    id = id,      # <-- first occurrence
    seed = seed,
    id = id       # <-- duplicate
  )
}
```

## Fix

Remove the first `id = id` in each affected constructor, keeping only the one after `seed`.

title: "empty selection prep/bake is a no-op" test always passes due to self-comparison
description:
## Issue

The "empty selection prep/bake is a no-op" test in every step's test file contains a self-comparison that always passes, making the test meaningless:

```r
test_that("empty selection prep/bake is a no-op", {
  rec1 <- recipe(mpg ~ ., mtcars)
  rec2 <- step_smote(rec1)

  rec1 <- prep(rec1, mtcars)
  rec2 <- prep(rec2, mtcars)

  baked1 <- bake(rec1, mtcars)
  baked2 <- bake(rec2, mtcars)

  expect_identical(baked1, baked1)  # compares baked1 to itself, not to baked2!
})
```

`expect_identical(baked1, baked1)` will always pass regardless of whether the step is actually a no-op. The assertion should be `expect_identical(baked1, baked2)`.

## Affected files

- `tests/testthat/test-smote.R`
- `tests/testthat/test-bsmote.R`
- `tests/testthat/test-adasyn.R`
- `tests/testthat/test-nearmiss.R`
- `tests/testthat/test-rose.R`
- `tests/testthat/test-smotenc.R`
- `tests/testthat/test-tomek.R`
- `tests/testthat/test-upsample.R`
- `tests/testthat/test-downsample.R`

## Fix

Change `expect_identical(baked1, baked1)` to `expect_identical(baked1, baked2)` in all affected test files.

title: test-tomek.R "bad data" tests exercise step_smote instead of step_tomek
description:
## Issue

The "bad data" test in `tests/testthat/test-tomek.R` calls `step_smote()` instead of `step_tomek()`, so it is testing the wrong step:

```r
test_that("bad data", {
  rec <- recipe(~., data = circle_example)
  # numeric check
  expect_snapshot(
    error = TRUE,
    rec |>
      step_smote(x) |>   # should be step_tomek

  )
  # Multiple variable check
  expect_snapshot(
    error = TRUE,
    rec |>

      prep()
  )
})
```

The snapshot file `tests/testthat/_snaps/tomek.md` therefore contains SMOTE error messages rather than Tomek error messages. This test provides no coverage of `step_tomek()`'s input validation.

Replace `step_smote` with `step_tomek` in both snapshot calls, then update the snapshot with `testthat::snapshot_review()` or by deleting the relevant entries in `_snaps/tomek.md` and re-running the tests.

title: No tests for NA values in outcome variable for step_upsample() and step_downsample()
description:
## Issue

Both `step_upsample()` and `step_downsample()` document that `NA` values in the outcome variable are handled (missing rows are selected at random alongside the other levels). However, there are no tests exercising this code path.

This is especially important given that the NA-handling code in both steps contains a bug (see #177) that would only be caught by such a test.

## Missing tests

`tests/testthat/test-upsample.R` and `tests/testthat/test-downsample.R` should each include a test along the lines of:

```r
test_that("NA values in outcome are handled", {
  df <- data.frame(
    x = 1:10,
    class = factor(c(NA, "A", "A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B", "B", "B"))
  )

  result <- recipe(~., data = df) |>
    step_upsample(class) |>
    prep() |>
    bake(new_data = NULL)

  # NA rows should be preserved and resampled
  expect_true(any(is.na(result$class)))
  # majority class should be balanced up
  expect_equal(
    sort(table(result$class, useNA = "no")),
    sort(table(df$class, useNA = "no"))
  )
})
```

title: step_upsample() and step_downsample() error when outcome variable contains NA
description:
## Bug

`step_upsample()` and `step_downsample()` document support for `NA` values in the outcome variable, but both steps error at bake time when NAs are actually present.

## Minimal example

```r
library(recipes)
library(themis)

df <- data.frame(
  x = 1:10,
  class = factor(c(NA, "A", "A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B", "B", "B"))
)

recipe(~., data = df) |>
  step_upsample(class) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL)
#> Error in supsamp(missing, object$target) : 
#>   argument "num" is missing, with no default
```

## Root cause

In `bake.step_upsample()` and `bake.step_downsample()`, rows with `NA` in the outcome are separated out and then resampled at the end:

```r
# R/upsample.R
if (!is.null(missing)) {
  new_data <- bind_rows(new_data, supsamp(missing, object$target))
}
```

But `supsamp()` is defined as `supsamp <- function(x, wts, num)` — it requires three arguments. The call only passes two (`x = missing`, `wts = object$target`), leaving `num` missing.

The same bug exists in `bake.step_downsample()`:

```r
# R/downsample.R
if (!is.null(missing)) {
  new_data <- bind_rows(new_data, subsamp(missing, object$target))
}
```

## Fix

The missing rows should be sampled with uniform weights and up to `object$target` rows:

```r
# upsample
supsamp(missing, wts = rep(1, nrow(missing)), num = object$target)

# downsample
subsamp(missing, wts = rep(1, nrow(missing)), num = object$target)
```

### Tips for a helpful bug report: 

 * Please include a **minimal reproducible example,** a reprex, to demonstrate the bug. If you've never heard of a reprex before, start by reading "[What is a reprex](https://github.com/tidyverse/reprex#what-is-a-reprex)" and following the advice there. If we can't reproduce a bug, we can't fit it. 

 * Here is a good example bug report: [#46](https://github.com/tidymodels/tune/issues/46)

title: step_smote breaks with some over_ratios
description:
## The problem

`step_smote` throws an error when a class is marginally below the target upsampling threshold. This only occurs in rare cases when smote tries to synthesize a fraction of a sample (n < 1).

The issue occurs in `themis:::smote_impl`. When `samples_needed` contains a number smaller than 1, `themis:::smote_data` returns an empty matrix, subsequently causing an error at the line `out_df[var] <- data[[names(samples_needed)[i]]][[var]][1]`

One quick solution might be to `floor` the `ratio_target` when checking which classes need to be upsampled in `themis:::smote_impl`, as below. This would ignore the variables fractionally below the target threshold.
`which_upsample <- which(table(df[[var]]) < ratio_target) # orig`
`which_upsample <- which(table(df[[var]]) < floor(ratio_target)) # possible solution`

## Reproducible example
``` r
library(recipes)
library(themis)
set.seed(123)

dat <- data.frame(
    outcome = c(rep("X", 101), rep("Z", 50)),
    X1 = rnorm(151))

rec_49 <- recipe(outcome ~ ., data = head(dat)) |>
    step_smote(outcome, over_ratio = 0.49, seed = 231)

    step_smote(outcome, over_ratio = 0.5, seed = 231)
```

title: Update to use print_step() instead of printer() in print methods
description:
Hello 👋 

In the most recent [CRAN release](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/recipes/index.html) of {recipes}, we took the first step towards [updating the printing infrastructure to use {cli}](https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/issues/426). This means that in order for your steps to print properly when the next version of {recipes} gets on CRAN, you will need to have adopted this change as well. Failure to do so won't result in errors, only malformed printing. The change itself is fairly minimal. Please see the following PR https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/pull/871 for examples of how this change is to be done. Please let me know if you have any questions!

See example below:

```r
# Old
print.step_pls <- function(x, width = max(20, options()$width - 35), ...) {
  cat("PLS feature extraction with ")
  printer(x$columns, x$terms, x$trained, width = width)
  invisible(x)
}

# New
print.step_pls <- function(x, width = max(20, options()$width - 35), ...) {
  title <- "PLS feature extraction with "
  print_step(x$columns, x$terms, x$trained, width = width, title = title)
  invisible(x)
}
```

using step_tomek with ID variables
description:
## The problem

I'm having trouble using `themis::step_tomek()` with an ID variable. `step_tomek()` seems to ignore the variable roles defined in the recipe, which `step_smote()` in comparison does not.  

## Reproducible example

```r
library(recipes)
library(themis)
library(dplyr)

# prepare data
data <- circle_example %>% 
  mutate(id = as.character(row_number())) %>% 
  as_tibble()

# define recipe with SMOTE step
rec_smote <- recipe(class~., data = data) %>% 
  update_role(id, new_role = "id") %>% 
  step_smote(class)

# bake
rec_smote %>% 
  prep() %>% 
  bake(new_data = NULL)
#> # A tibble: 684 × 4
#>        x     y id    class 
#>    <dbl> <dbl> <fct> <fct> 
#>  1  2.59 10.6  1     Rest  
#>  2  9.71  6.83 2     Circle
#>  3  9.53 11.6  3     Rest  
#>  4  9.73 11.9  4     Rest  
#>  5 13.1   9.03 5     Rest  
#>  6  9.96  3.64 6     Rest  
#>  7  1.13 11.6  7     Rest  
#>  8  4.26  2.30 8     Rest  
#>  9 10.3   9.71 9     Circle
#> 10  8.20  6.82 10    Circle
#> # … with 674 more rows

# define recipe with TOMEK step
rec_tomek <- recipe(class~., data = data) %>% 
  update_role(id, new_role = "id") %>% 
  step_tomek(class)

# bake
rec_tomek %>% 
  prep() %>% 
  bake(new_data = NULL)
#> Error: All columns selected for the step should be numeric
```
While `step_smote()` executes properly with the character-variable defined as "id"-column, `step_tomek()`does not and returns an error: `Error: All columns selected for the step should be numeric`. 

Is this expected behaviour? It appears a similar bug for `step_smote()` has already been discussed and squashed here: https://github.com/tidymodels/themis/issues/20. 
I also get the same error when adding the recipe to a workflow and fitting a model without prepping and baking the recipe first.

title: Support for categorical variables in step_rose and friends
description:
First, thank you for creating this package! I just had a question/request.

I’ll preface this by saying I am not super familiar with all of the underpinnings of the SMOTE and ROSE algorithms. However, based on what I’ve read online about the underlying packages that themis uses, it appears these algorithms can handle categorical variables. Again, I’m not sure HOW they handle them (convert to dummy and then round to the nearest integer?) but it appears it’s possible. 

My question is, is there a specific reason (eg don’t agree with how they’re handled) step_rose and others don’t support data with categorical features? I know you currently can convert to dummy and then pass the data in but the results when you juice the data are values like 0.76 for a 0/1 dummy variable.

Is it possible to implement the same method that the ROSE package uses for categorical variables?

Again, I could be misunderstanding how it’s done currently so please correct me where needed.

Thanks!

title: Factor level orders are reversed or lost in some `step_` functions
description:
I've been noticing issues with `step_rose()` such that when applied in a two class classification with factor variables, the factor variable in the predictions have the levels in the wrong order.

This has impacts down the line in yardstick for metrics that are not symmetric with factor level order such as `pr_auc`, so I've had to work around this by fixing the factor levels and recomputing the metrics, which I don't want to keep doing in the future.

After searching around to find what was causing this, it is that the factors are reversed in `step_rose()` to the majority class.

I've written some tests to isolate the problem, checked they failed, then fixed them. While I was originally intending to fix `step_rose()`, it turns out that `step_nearmiss()` and `step_tomek` are also affected. The _fix_ is applied in this package as a safety net, however if the fix is applied to upstream packages as well ([RANN](https://github.com/jefferislab/RANN), [ROSE](https://github.com/cran/ROSE) and [unbalanced](https://github.com/dalpozz/unbalanced)), then the solution here will still hold.

title: Distinguish between generated and original data
description:
Thanks for this cool package. I think in general with upsampling, it would be useful to know if an observation was part of the original data or (artificially) generated with the upsampling method. E.g. for inspecting if the method is working as expected. Borrowing from an example in the doc, I could not figure out how to do this.

Of course, I can 
```r
setdiff(juiced, credit_data[, names(juiced)])
```
But that's hacky  and slow for large data.

I don't know the recipes / themis API very well, but it seems as we could fix this as follows: if `role` was not set to `NA`, we could create a new column that contains the indication. If `NA`, the default, we don't. Alternatively, if one can specify which variables are used for upsampling (I think currently all are used), then, the distinction would also be possible (because NA would be filled in the columns not used). Unfortunately, there is only one `...` allowed in a function declaration, which is already used to specify *one* target variable for upsampling. title: How to handle id-variables when upsampling
description:
Currency steps in themis will use the whole dataset when upsampling and downsampling. This is not much of an issue in `step_upsample()` and `step_downsample()`. But it becomes an issue if you specify an ID variable and use steps such as `step_smote()` and `step_rose()` as they produce synthetic observations.

As I see it there are 2 ways to deal with this

- Make the steps unable to work with id variables
- Have upsampling steps populate non-predictor variables with NAs

Something has to be done since the current implementation can introduce bias by letting the id variable be part of the space.
